To: Executive Leadership, Supply Chain and Operations
From: Sustainability & Logistics Director
Date: Today
Subject: Balancing delivered cost and carbon footprint in warehouse-to-store shipping

Context
Our warehouse-to-store network must deliver reliably while advancing our sustainability commitments. Each shipping route in our network carries two per-unit metrics: a monetary transportation cost and a carbon emission rate. These metrics often move in opposite directions—routes that are attractive on price can be more carbon-intensive—so we need a practical method to balance spend and footprint without compromising service.

Operational rules we must honor
- Route activation and setup: Using any new warehouse-to-store route requires an upfront setup cost covering contract initiation, regulatory documentation, and loading-dock readiness. A route is either active or not; once active, the setup cost applies regardless of shipped volume.
- Minimum order quantities: Activated routes must carry at least a defined number of units to justify line-haul utilization and handling. Partial loads are not accepted on these lanes.
- Supplier limits per store: To keep receiving operations manageable and vendor management efficient, each store may receive deliveries from no more than a set number of warehouses within the planning window.

Supply and demand guardrails
- Each warehouse has a firm inventory limit available for shipment during the planning period; we cannot ship more than is available.
- Each store has a minimum demand requirement that must be met to protect service levels.

Management priority and trade-offs
Leadership has established importance weights that place greater emphasis on transportation cost than on emissions, while still valuing carbon reductions. To compare candidate plans, we will calculate a combined score in which:
- Variable shipping costs are scaled by the cost weight.
- Total route emissions are scaled by the emissions weight.
- Upfront setup costs for any activated routes are included at full value and are not scaled by weights.
This approach allows us to transparently navigate the tension between price and carbon while accounting for the real costs of opening lanes.

Business goal and decision outputs
We will identify which routes to activate and how much to ship on each active route so that:
- Warehouse supplies are not exceeded and each store’s demand is fully covered.
- Any activated route ships at least the required minimum order.
- Each store receives from no more than the allowed number of warehouses.
Among all feasible plans that satisfy these rules, we will recommend the plan with the lowest combined score under the stated weights. The output will be an actionable lane activation list and shipment quantities by route that can be executed by Transportation and Store Operations.

Next steps
- Validate the inputs in the annex with Regional DCs and Merchandising.
- Run the scenario and review results with Finance and ESG to confirm the balance between budget impact and emissions reduction.
- Confirm the activation plan with carrier partners and align receiving schedules with stores.

Annex — Data (planning inputs)
- Number of source warehouses: {NUM_SOURCES}
- Number of destination stores: {NUM_DESTINATIONS}
- Warehouse supplies (units by source): {SUPPLIES}
- Store demand requirements (units by destination): {DEMANDS}
- Variable shipping cost per unit by route (source→destination): {COST_MATRIX}
- CO2 emissions per unit by route (source→destination): {EMISSION_MATRIX}
- Cost importance weight: {WEIGHT_COST}
- Emission importance weight: {WEIGHT_EMISSION}
- Upfront setup costs per route: {FIXED_COSTS}
- Minimum order quantities per activated route (units): {MIN_ORDER_QUANTITIES}
- Maximum suppliers allowed per store: {MAX_SUPPLIERS_PER_STORE}
